clue.text: Badger given a Japanese drink in Japan

definitions.note: a place in Japan: the definition locates rather than names

parts.note: to badger someone is to pester them
taken as written
a variant spelling of sake, Japanese rice wine

explanation.surface: Someone pestered into accepting a drink of rice wine while visiting Japan.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is just 'in Japan': the answer is a city there, and the drink is spelt SAKI rather than the usual sake.
explanation.definitionFit: Nagasaki is a port city on the southern island of Kyushu, so it is a place located within that country.

clue.text: (and 3) Raise capital for writer

definitions.note: the writer's first name; his surname is the answer at 3

parts.note: to lift, as a car is lifted with a hydraulic tool
this half of the wordplay supplies the linked answer at 3 down

explanation.surface: Raising money to fund an author.
explanation.walkthrough: '(and 3)' links this entry to 3 down: the clue gives JACK LONDON, a verb for raise plus the British capital.
explanation.definitionFit: Jack London was the American novelist who wrote The Call of the Wild and White Fang.

clue.text: See 2

definitions.note: a cross-reference: the writer defined at 2 down, of whom this is the surname

wordplay.note: points to the clue at 2 down, where 'capital' is the United Kingdom's capital city

explanation.walkthrough: The clue at 2 down covers both entries: 'Raise' gives the first name and 'capital' gives this surname.
explanation.definitionFit: Together with the entry at 2 this completes the name of the American author of The Call of the Wild.

clue.text: A bed bug?

parts.note: surface reading: an insect such as a bedbug that lives in mattresses
setter's reading: something in bed that bugs, or annoys, a sleeping partner

explanation.walkthrough: 'Bug' is a verb in disguise: the thing that bugs you in bed is a noisy partner's breathing.
explanation.definitionFit: Loud breathing during sleep is the classic nuisance that keeps a bedmate awake, so it irritates people in bed.

clue.text: Halpern's broken into little pieces

indicators.note: something broken is smashed apart, so its letters are reassembled in a fresh order

parts.note: the name with its S, taken letter for letter

explanation.surface: Someone called Halpern has been smashed to bits.
explanation.definitionFit: Shrapnel is the scattered metal fragments thrown out by an exploding shell, so it is small broken bits.

clue.text: Serenaded girls in beach wear

parts.note: a serenade is sung to someone
lasses are girls, especially in northern Britain

explanation.surface: Young women in swimsuits being sung to on the sand.
explanation.definitionFit: Dark protective eyewear is something people put on at the seaside, so it is worn on the beach.

clue.text: Coastal vehicle lolloped along for a stretch

indicators.note: a stretch is a continuous run, so the letters are taken as an unbroken span across the words

parts.note: the run of letters spanning the end of one word and the start of the next

explanation.surface: A seaside vehicle lumbering clumsily along the shore for a while.
explanation.definitionFit: A pedalo is a small pedal-powered boat hired out at seaside resorts, so it is a craft used along the coast.

clue.text: King in Portuguese province once, once halved a biscuit

indicators.note: the king's letter sits inside the name of the former colony

parts.note: Macao was a Portuguese territory until 1999
R for rex, Latin for king

indicators.note: cut in half, so only the first two of its four letters remain

parts.note: taken as written before cutting

explanation.surface: A monarch in a former Portuguese colony once broke a biscuit in two.
explanation.walkthrough: The first 'once' belongs to the province description; the second is the word cut in half.
explanation.definitionFit: A macaroon is a small sweet almond or coconut cake classed as a cookie or biscuit.

clue.text: Something you wouldn't stake on a lottery, or bingo!

definitions.text: Something you wouldn't stake on a lottery
definitions.meaning: first meaning: 'betting the ...' is risking everything, which no sensible person does on a lottery
second meaning: the call a winning player shouts in the game of bingo

explanation.surface: Gambling talk: don't bet everything on a lottery ticket, or on the bingo hall either.
explanation.walkthrough: In British bingo, a player with a full card calls out 'House!' to claim the win.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the home you would never wager, and also the traditional shout claiming a full card in the game.

clue.text: Explorer, in a flash, heading off

indicators.note: the head of the word, its first letter, is taken off

parts.note: a spark is a brief flash of light

explanation.surface: An adventurer setting off at once, in an instant.
explanation.walkthrough: Mungo Park was the Scottish explorer of the Niger river.
explanation.definitionFit: Mungo Park was an eighteenth-century Scottish traveller who charted the course of the Niger in West Africa.

clue.text: Study scripture, getting upset about a character who gave his soul away

definitions.text: a character who gave his soul away

indicators.note: goes about means wraps around, so one piece encloses the next

parts.note: to do a subject at school is to study it
RI is religious instruction, the school subject
upset in the sense of cross
taken as written

explanation.surface: A student of the Bible grows cross about a figure who sold his soul.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Upset' looks like an anagram signal but is a plain synonym for cross; RI is religious instruction, the school lesson.
explanation.definitionFit: Oscar Wilde's hero wishes his portrait would age instead of him, in effect trading his soul for eternal youth.

clue.text: Jester backing a popular Arthurian knight

indicators.note: going backwards, so the word for a joker is read from its end

parts.note: a wag is a joker
taken as written
in fashion, popular

explanation.surface: A court fool supporting a well-liked knight of the Round Table.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Gawain, nephew of King Arthur, is one of the Round Table knights, hero of the Green Knight poem.

clue.text: Dropped on 1, I caught many people up in a grave situation

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: the other letters are placed inside the burial word

parts.note: a tomb is a grave
taken as written
c is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for caught

indicators.note: in a down clue, going up means the word is read from bottom to top

parts.note: a mob is a crowd

explanation.surface: Someone caught up with a crowd in a serious predicament.
explanation.walkthrough: 1 refers to the answer at 1 down; I, C and the reversed crowd go inside the grave, preceded by A.
explanation.definitionFit: In August 1945 a nuclear weapon was released over the Japanese port, three days after Hiroshima.

clue.text: Entire meal pushed aside, we hear, north of Coventry

definitions.note: the definition locates the place rather than naming it

indicators.note: what we hear is spoken, so the phrase counts by its sound

parts.note: a meal pushed away untouched has had none of it eaten

explanation.surface: A diner rejects a whole meal somewhere in the Midlands.
explanation.walkthrough: Nuneaton is a Warwickshire town a few miles north of the city of Coventry in England's Midlands.
explanation.definitionFit: Nuneaton is a market town in Warwickshire lying just above Coventry on the map, so it is found to its north.

clue.text: A tour of Romanic island

indicators.note: a tour wanders around, so the letters go round in a new order

parts.note: taken letter for letter

explanation.surface: A sightseeing trip around a Romance-speaking island.
explanation.definitionFit: Minorca, or Menorca, is one of Spain's Balearic Islands in the western Mediterranean Sea.

clue.text: Further education placement, which isn''t a growth area

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the British system that matches students without a university place to unfilled courses after exam results
second meaning: an open space in a wood where no trees grow

explanation.surface: A college place offered in a subject with poor prospects.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Growth area' sounds like business jargon; here it means literal plant growth.
explanation.definitionFit: It names both the UCAS process allocating leftover university places and a treeless gap in a forest.

clue.text: The most stuffy has to pay the costs in court

indicators.note: the losing party's word is set inside the abbreviation for court

parts.note: CT is a standard abbreviation for court
in a lawsuit, the side that loses is usually ordered to pay the costs

explanation.surface: The most pompous person ends up footing the legal bill.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stuffy' suggests pompous, but here it is used of air: close weather is humid and airless.
explanation.definitionFit: Close describes air that is warm and stale, so the superlative form means stuffiest.

clue.text: Shed's artistry, plus something charged

parts.note: artistry is skill
an ion is an atom carrying an electrical charge

explanation.surface: A garden building praised for its craftsmanship and its price.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shed' can be a verb (cast off), but here it is the noun; the 's stands for 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: A skillion is an Australian term for a lean-to outbuilding with a single sloping roof.

clue.text: Inaction because the French invades

indicators.note: an invader moves into territory, so one piece goes inside another

parts.note: since means because
le is the masculine French for 'the'

explanation.surface: Doing nothing because the French have invaded.
explanation.definitionFit: Inaction here means absence of activity or sound; keeping silent is doing and saying nothing.

clue.text: Bone being consumed by drink, one acquired disease

indicators.note: something consumed is taken inside, so the first piece goes into the drink

parts.note: beer is a drink
a rib is a bone
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A drinker swallowed a bone and caught an illness.
explanation.definitionFit: Beriberi is a nutritional illness caused by a lack of vitamin B1, thiamine.

clue.text: Antelopes — those at the back end of camels?

indicators.note: the back end of a word is its tail, so only its closing letters are used

parts.note: the closing three letters of the word
the letters are read out as a spoken list, with 'and' before the last one

explanation.surface: Antelopes trailing behind a camel train.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters at the end of 'camels' are E, L and S; say 'E, L and S' aloud as a list and it spells the plural.
explanation.definitionFit: Elands are large African antelopes with spiralled horns, the biggest of the antelope species.

clue.text: Philanthropist takes the biscuit a la mode

parts.note: a rusk is a hard dry biscuit
a la mode means fashionable, in

explanation.surface: A benefactor surpasses everyone at being fashionable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Takes the biscuit' is a British idiom for being the most outrageous; here it is split. John Ruskin funded many social causes.
explanation.definitionFit: John Ruskin, the Victorian critic, gave away his inherited fortune to charitable and educational schemes.

clue.text: Charge again when bread's short and overdrawn?

parts.note: an overdrawn account is in the red

indicators.note: cut short, so the word loses its final letter

parts.note: a loaf of bread

explanation.surface: Asking to be billed again when money is tight and the account is overdrawn.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bread' is slang for money, but here it is a loaf, shortened and placed inside the colour of debt.
explanation.definitionFit: To reload a gun is to put a fresh charge of ammunition in it, so it means charge again.

clue.text: Bank prudently in south-east 3

definitions.note: a district located within the area named at 3

parts.note: a camber is the banked slope of a road
to act well is to act sensibly

explanation.surface: A financial institution acting cautiously in the south-east.
explanation.walkthrough: 3 points to the answer at 3 down, the capital; 'Bank' looks financial but is a road's slope.
explanation.definitionFit: Camberwell is a district of south London, lying in the SE5 postal area of the capital.

clue.text: See 25

definitions.note: a cross-reference: the driver defined at 25 across, of whom this is the surname

wordplay.note: points to the clue at 25 across, where 'incline' is a slope

explanation.walkthrough: The clue at 25 covers both entries: the reversed traveller gives the first name and 'incline' gives this surname.
explanation.definitionFit: Together with the entry at 25 this completes the name of the British racing driver who was 1996 world champion.

clue.text: Native Americans get lost endlessly

indicators.note: without an end, so the final letter is dropped

parts.note: 'hop it!' is British slang for go away

explanation.surface: Indigenous people told to go away forever.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hop it' is a British dismissal meaning clear off.
explanation.definitionFit: The Hopi are a Pueblo people of north-eastern Arizona, one of the tribes of the American Southwest.

clue.text: (and 24) He drove Traveller backwards onto incline

definitions.note: the driver's first name; his surname is the answer at 24

indicators.note: read in the opposite direction, from last letter to first

parts.note: a nomad is a traveller
this part of the wordplay supplies the linked answer at 24 across

explanation.surface: A driver steered a wanderer in reverse up a slope.
explanation.walkthrough: '(and 24)' links this entry to 24 across: the clue gives DAMON HILL, the Formula One world champion of 1996.
explanation.definitionFit: Damon Hill was a racing driver who won the 1996 Formula One title, so he drove for a living.

clue.text: Back the winner

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to support a cause
second meaning: the victor of a contest

explanation.walkthrough: It reads like betting advice; the two parts are a verb meaning support and a noun for the victor.
explanation.definitionFit: As a verb it means to support or advocate; as a noun it is the one who finishes first in a competition.
